chapter_title: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 6 periods = 270 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 4h 30min

periods.stage_label: Wonder and Question — noticing phenomena and posing investigable questions
periods.activity_title: What Makes You Curious? Framing Scientific Questions
periods.activity_description: Students explore the chapter's opening curiosity questions — the thinner side of a puri, sand grains versus stars, biological diversity — and attempt to reframe their personal wonderings as investigable scientific questions, distinguishing those that can be tested from those that cannot.

roles.role_description: Draws student attention to each curiosity prompt in turn, probing which questions feel testable and why, without resolving the answers.
Records their own curiosity question in the space provided and attempts to restate it as a question that could be investigated with available means.
Share their questions within a small group and collectively sort them into 'could investigate' and 'would need much more' categories, justifying each placement.

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the three opening curiosity prompts aloud and invites brief initial reactions without evaluating them, establishing that wondering is the starting point of science.

Students individually write their own curiosity question and then attempt to rewrite it as something observable or testable, guided by the teacher's prompt: 'What would you need to see, measure, or change?'
Groups share questions and sort them into two categories — investigable now versus requiring far more resources — justifying each decision to each other.
A whole-class share-out surfaces two or three questions from each category; the teacher uses student language to name what makes a question investigable without supplying the formal vocabulary yet.
The teacher briefly signals that the next unit will take one familiar phenomenon — a puri puffing — and show exactly how a good investigable question is built from it.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit sets the chapter's tone: science begins with genuine curiosity, not with a pre-given experiment. Watch for students who treat every question as either trivially easy or impossibly hard — the common error is assuming 'investigable' means 'answerable in one go', whereas the chapter argues that even a simple kitchen question can remain partially open. Encourage groups to debate borderline cases rather than settle them quickly, since productive disagreement here mirrors real scientific practice.
materials: Notebook or loose paper for individual writing

periods.stage_label: Identify Variables — distinguishing what can be changed, controlled, and observed
periods.activity_description: Students map the puri investigation from the chapter onto a variables framework, physically sorting labelled cards representing factors — dough thickness, oil temperature, flour type, entry angle, puri size — into 'can change', 'must keep the same', and 'what we observe or measure' columns on their desks.

roles.role_description: Introduces the puri phenomenon briefly, then distributes the factor cards and monitors group sorting without revealing the 'correct' placement until groups have committed to their arrangement.
Sort the factor cards into the three columns collaboratively, debating which factors are variables and which are outcomes, and recording their reasoning in writing.

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the puri scenario from the chapter aloud and asks students what they noticed — focusing attention on the phenomenon of puffing and the asymmetry of thickness — connecting to the wondering work of the previous unit.

Groups receive a set of labelled factor cards and arrange them across three column headers on their desk or sheet: 'What we can change', 'What we keep the same', and 'What we observe or measure', discussing each card before placing it.

Groups rotate to view another group's arrangement and leave a written sticky-note challenge questioning any placement they disagree with, then return to read the challenges left on their own arrangement.

Whole-class discussion resolves contested placements using the chapter's own language — controllable variables versus observable outcomes — with the teacher naming these terms after students have articulated the distinction in their own words.
Teacher previews that the next unit will ask: once variables are sorted, how do you design the actual test?

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the questioning work of the previous unit by giving students a concrete phenomenon to analyse. The most common confusion here is between a factor that could be observed (like whether oil splatters) and one that is the intended outcome of the investigation — students tend to lump all observations into one category rather than distinguishing incidental from targeted ones; the chapter explicitly notes that unexpected sensory details like splattering should still be recorded. Let groups commit to their arrangement before discussion so the reasoning process is visible.
materials: Labelled factor cards (teacher-prepared: strips of paper naming dough thickness, oil temperature, flour type, entry angle, puri size, puffing time, whether it puffs)
Desk space or A3 sheet divided into three columns
Sticky notes or small paper slips for inter-group challenges

periods.stage_label: Design a Controlled Experiment — applying the one-variable principle to plan a test
periods.activity_title: Plan the Test: Changing Only One Thing
periods.activity_description: Students use the sorted variables from the previous unit to design a written experimental plan for one specific question about the puri investigation, applying the chapter's principle of changing only one variable at a time while keeping all others constant, and specifying how they would record observations.

roles.role_description: Collaboratively draft an experimental plan specifying: the question being tested, which single variable changes, what is kept constant, and how observations will be recorded — including unexpected details.

Circulates and uses probing questions to push groups to specify rather than generalise — asking 'how will you know the temperature is different?' or 'what exactly will you write down?' without writing the plan for them.

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly revisits the three-column variable sort from the previous unit and poses the design challenge: 'Choose one variable to change and write a plan that would actually let you test its effect on puffing.'

Groups draft their experimental plan on a structured planning sheet with prompts: our question, the one thing we change, what we keep the same, what we measure or observe, and how we will record it — including any unexpected observations.

Groups exchange plans and evaluate each other's plan against one criterion at a time: Does it change only one variable? Does it specify what stays constant? Does it name a recording method? Written feedback is given on the plan sheet itself.

Two or three plans are shared with the class; the teacher highlights how the chapter's oil-temperature example (three temperatures, same dough, same angle) matches the one-variable principle and connects student plans to this model.
Teacher signals that a real investigation rarely ends at one planned test — the next unit examines what happens when results arrive and generate new questions.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently write plans that change two things at once — for example, testing a different flour and a different oil temperature simultaneously — because this feels like 'doing more'. The chapter is explicit that this is the key error in experimental design: it makes results uninterpretable. Prompt groups caught doing this with: 'If the result is different, which change caused it?' rather than telling them directly. The peer-evaluation step is critical here because students notice this error more readily in others' plans than in their own.
materials: Experimental planning sheet (teacher-prepared with five prompt fields)

periods.stage_label: Design a Controlled Experiment — applying the one-variable principle to plan a test
periods.activity_title: Recording Well: What Counts as an Observation?
periods.activity_description: Students examine what complete observation recording looks like by analysing the chapter's guidance on noting unexpected sensory details — splattering, smoke, smell — alongside the targeted measurement, then revise their experimental plans to include a richer, more complete observation record.

roles.role_description: Leads a structured discussion drawing directly on the chapter's emphasis that all observations — including unexpected ones — should be recorded, using the oil-splattering example to anchor the point.

Revises their group's plan from the previous unit to add at least two additional observation columns — one targeted, one for unexpected details — and writes a brief justification for each column added.

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the chapter's recording guidance aloud, pausing at the splattering and smoking examples, and asks: 'Why would a scientist bother writing down something they weren't looking for?' — collecting student responses before offering the chapter's reasoning.

Students individually revise their experimental plan's recording section, adding at least one targeted observation column and one column for unexpected details, writing a one-sentence justification for each addition.

A think-pair-share structure: students compare their revised recording plans with a partner and discuss whether the unexpected-details column could ever become the main variable in a future investigation, linking to the chapter's point about iteration.

Teacher draws together the key insight: good recording is not just accuracy but completeness, because unexpected observations are often the seed of the next investigation — as illustrated by the chapter's examples of fresh-versus-stored dough and pricking a hole before frying.
Teacher signals that the next unit will explore this iterative quality directly: how one completed investigation produces the questions for the next.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit continues the design work of the previous unit by deepening the recording dimension, so connect explicitly to the plans already drafted. The misconception to watch for is that 'unexpected' means 'wrong' — students sometimes believe that noting oil-splattering is an admission that something went wrong with the experiment rather than a sign of good scientific vigilance. The chapter explicitly frames unexpected observations as valuable, and this is worth restating in your own words when the think-pair-share discussion stalls.
materials: Students' experimental plans from the previous unit

periods.stage_label: Iterate — using observations to generate new questions and refine investigations
periods.activity_title: What Did the Result Open? Designing the Follow-Up Question
periods.activity_description: Students are presented with a set of hypothetical puri investigation results and must identify which result is most surprising, explain why it is surprising given the original question, generate one new investigable question it raises, and sketch a revised experimental plan to address that new question.

roles.role_description: Presents the hypothetical results set and asks students to treat them as if they were their own results, modelling how a scientist reacts to unexpected findings by pausing at each result and thinking aloud briefly.

Analyse the results collaboratively, identify the most surprising finding, produce one new investigable question, and sketch a follow-up experimental plan — applying the one-variable and complete-recording principles from the previous two units.

time_bands.activity: The teacher presents a simple hypothetical results table on the board: three oil temperatures tested, puffing outcomes noted, with one surprising result — the puri puffed faster at the intermediate temperature than the highest — and asks students to react before any analysis begins.

Groups analyse the hypothetical results, identify which finding is most surprising and state why in writing, then generate one new investigable question the surprising result raises — connecting to the chapter's examples of fresh-versus-stored dough and the pricked puri.

Groups sketch a revised experimental plan for their new question, applying the one-variable principle and the complete observation-recording approach from the previous two units, writing it on the reverse of their original plan sheet.
A representative from each group presents their new question and the key design choice they made; the class evaluates whether the one-variable principle is maintained in each proposal.

Teacher closes by naming the iterative cycle explicitly: observation → question → plan → result → new observation — and signals that the final unit will bring the whole arc together across the year's broader content.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the pivot of the arc: it asks students to treat a result not as an endpoint but as the beginning of the next investigation — the defining feature of scientific inquiry as the chapter presents it. The misconception to watch for is that a surprising result means the experiment 'failed'; the chapter is explicit that these are the most productive results because they open new questions, such as the pricked-puri example. Ensure groups write their new question before they sketch the plan, so the question genuinely drives the design rather than the design being recycled from the previous unit with superficial changes.
materials: Hypothetical results table (teacher-prepared, written on board or distributed as a slip)
Students' plan sheets from previous units
homework: Choose one phenomenon from the chapter's year-preview — rising dough, the Moon's phases, or another that interests you — and write two questions about it: one that you could investigate with things available at home or school, and one that would need much more. Explain in one sentence what makes each question belong in its category.

periods.stage_label: Synthesise — applying the full inquiry cycle to evaluate and refine an investigation
periods.activity_title: The Investigator's Lens: Evaluating Any Investigation
periods.activity_description: Students apply the complete inquiry framework — question formulation, variable identification, controlled design, systematic recording, and iteration — to evaluate a short written investigation scenario drawn from the chapter, identifying what the investigator did well, what they missed, and what follow-up question their results suggest.

roles.role_description: Presents the evaluation scenario and leads a structured whole-class synthesis that names the full cycle of scientific inquiry as a unified practice, drawing on the puri worked example and connecting it to the year's broader content arc.

Reads the scenario independently, completes a four-part written evaluation — question quality, variable control, recording completeness, and iteration potential — then contributes to the whole-class discussion.

time_bands.activity: The teacher presents a short written scenario: an investigator tests whether dough thickness affects puffing by trying thin and thick dough, but changes the oil temperature between the two trials and notes only whether the puri puffed, recording nothing else. Students read it independently.

Students complete a four-part written evaluation: (1) Is the question investigable and focused? (2) Is only one variable changed? (3) Is the recording complete? (4) What new question do the results open? — using the framework built across this chapter's arc.

Whole-class discussion takes each evaluation criterion in turn; the teacher draws out student responses and connects each criterion to the chapter's content — question formulation, variable control, complete recording, iteration — naming the full inquiry cycle as an integrated practice.

Teacher broadens the synthesis: the same cycle — from a focused question through controlled design, complete observation, and iterative follow-up — applies whether the subject is a kitchen phenomenon, an electric circuit, the Moon's phases, or an ecosystem, previewing how this framework will serve students across the year.

Teacher closes with the chapter's own closing spirit — 'Happy investigating!' — affirming that the investigative habit of mind is the takeaway from this chapter and the foundation for all that follows.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws the entire chapter together and is designed to stand alone for any class that has worked through the chapter's content, so anchor the discussion in the scenario and the chapter's puri example rather than assuming any particular earlier activity. The most important thing to establish is that the four criteria — focused question, one-variable control, complete recording, iteration — form a single integrated cycle rather than a checklist of separate skills; the chapter itself models this unity in the puri worked example. Close by naming the connection between the kitchen investigation and planetary-scale questions explicitly, as the chapter does, to show students that the same investigative lens scales.
materials: Printed or board-displayed evaluation scenario (teacher-prepared, describing the flawed investigation)

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Wonder and Question — noticing phenomena and posing investigable questions
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students explore the chapter's curiosity prompts and practise converting personal wonderings into investigable scientific questions, sorting them by feasibility.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can restate a personal curiosity as an investigable scientific question and distinguish questions that can be tested with available means from those that cannot, giving a reason for each classification.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Identify Variables — distinguishing what can be changed, controlled, and observed
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students sort the factors of the puri investigation into controllable variables, constants, and observable outcomes, debating placements with peers and resolving contested cases using the chapter's vocabulary.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can sort the factors of a given investigation into controllable variables, constants, and observable outcomes, and justify each placement using the distinction between what is changed and what is measured.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Design a Controlled Experiment — applying the one-variable principle to plan a test
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students draft an experimental plan for a chosen puri question applying the one-variable principle, then revise it to include targeted and unexpected observation recording, peer-evaluating each other's plans against explicit design criteria.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can produce a written experimental plan that changes only one variable, specifies what is kept constant, and includes a recording scheme that captures both targeted measurements and unexpected observations, and can identify design flaws in another's plan.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Iterate — using observations to generate new questions and refine investigations
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students analyse hypothetical puri investigation results, identify the most surprising finding, generate a new investigable question it raises, and sketch a revised experimental plan to address it.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can identify a surprising finding in a set of investigation results, explain why it is unexpected in relation to the original question, and generate a new investigable question with a corresponding experimental plan that applies the one-variable and complete-recording principles.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Synthesise — applying the full inquiry cycle to evaluate and refine an investigation
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students evaluate a flawed written investigation scenario against all four inquiry criteria — focused question, variable control, recording completeness, and iteration potential — and synthesise the full cycle as an integrated practice applicable across scientific domains.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can evaluate a given investigation against the full scientific inquiry cycle — identifying strengths and flaws in question formulation, variable control, observation recording, and iteration — and propose a specific improvement for each identified flaw.

assessment_items.stage_label: Wonder and Question — noticing phenomena and posing investigable questions
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can restate a personal curiosity as an investigable scientific question and distinguish questions that can be tested with available means from those that cannot, giving a reason for each classification.

competency.competency_text: Formulate focused scientific questions, identify controllable and observable variables, design simple controlled experiments, and record observations systematically.

assessment_items.question_text: A student notices that dough left near a warm stove rises faster than dough kept on a cold countertop. Which of the following is the best investigable scientific question this observation could lead to?

options.label: A
options.text: Does the temperature at which dough is kept affect how fast it rises?

options.label: B
options.text: How is dough made in different countries?

options.label: C
options.text: Why is dough so interesting to study?

options.label: D
options.text: Will dough always rise if you wait long enough?

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this reveals the student has not grasped what makes a question investigable — it is personal interest rather than a testable relationship between variables.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this reveals a confusion between a yes/no existence question and a focused variable-relationship question; this question cannot be answered by a controlled test because 'always' is not bounded.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this reveals the student is treating the phenomenon as a cultural or descriptive topic rather than a scientific investigation — it is not testable by observation or experiment.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with written question formats may be asked to choose verbally between two options and explain their reasoning aloud. Students with stronger prior exposure can be asked to explain what change would be needed to make one of the distractors into an investigable question.

assessment_items.stage_label: Wonder and Question — noticing phenomena and posing investigable questions
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can restate a personal curiosity as an investigable scientific question and distinguish questions that can be tested with available means from those that cannot, giving a reason for each classification.

competency.competency_text: Formulate focused scientific questions, identify controllable and observable variables, design simple controlled experiments, and record observations systematically.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Question | Investigable with available means?
Why do some puri puff up more than others when fried? | ?
Are there more stars in the Milky Way than grains of sand on all Earth's beaches? | ?
Does the thickness of rolled dough affect whether a puri puffs? | ?
Why did the universe begin? | ?
assessment_items.question_text: A student tries to sort four questions into investigable and not easily investigable with school or home means. Refer to the table provided. Which row in the table is correctly sorted?

options.label: A
options.text: Row 1 — not easily investigable, because puri puffing requires special laboratory equipment

options.label: B
options.text: Row 2 — investigable, because it can be answered by counting carefully

options.label: C
options.text: Row 3 — investigable, because dough thickness can be changed and puffing can be observed

options.label: D
options.text: Row 4 — investigable, because scientists have already studied the origin of the universe

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this reveals the misconception that kitchen phenomena require formal laboratory equipment to investigate — the chapter explicitly states that a home kitchen provides sufficient opportunity.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this reveals confusion between a question being answerable in principle and being testable with available means; counting all grains and all stars is not feasible with school or home resources.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this reveals a confusion between a question being studied by scientists somewhere and a student being able to investigate it — the chapter distinguishes investigable-by-you from known-to-science.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the table format challenging can be asked to focus only on rows 3 and 4 and compare them verbally. Students who answer quickly can be asked to rewrite row 1 as an investigable version of the same curiosity.

assessment_items.stage_label: Identify Variables — distinguishing what can be changed, controlled, and observed
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can sort the factors of a given investigation into controllable variables, constants, and observable outcomes, and justify each placement using the distinction between what is changed and what is measured.

competency.competency_text: Formulate focused scientific questions, identify controllable and observable variables, design simple controlled experiments, and record observations systematically.

assessment_items.question_text: A student wants to test whether the type of flour (atta or maida) affects how well a puri puffs. She uses the same dough thickness, the same oil temperature, and the same entry angle for both trials, and records whether each puri puffs. In this investigation, what is the observable outcome?

options.label: A
options.text: The dough thickness

options.label: B
options.text: The oil temperature

options.label: C
options.text: The type of flour used

options.label: D
options.text: Whether the puri puffs or not

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this reveals a confusion between the controllable variable being tested and the observable outcome — the student has not yet separated what is changed from what is measured.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this reveals a confusion between a constant (what is kept the same) and an observable outcome — the student sees temperature as the focus because it is a quantity, not because it is measured.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this reveals the same constant-versus-outcome confusion as option B, suggesting the student has not yet internalised the three-category distinction.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the three-category framework abstract can be asked to answer a simpler preliminary question first: 'What does the student change? What does she watch for?' before being given the option set. Students who answer readily can be asked to identify one additional factor that would count as a constant in this investigation.

assessment_items.stage_label: Identify Variables — distinguishing what can be changed, controlled, and observed
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can sort the factors of a given investigation into controllable variables, constants, and observable outcomes, and justify each placement using the distinction between what is changed and what is measured.

competency.competency_text: Formulate focused scientific questions, identify controllable and observable variables, design simple controlled experiments, and record observations systematically.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Factor | Student's category
Oil temperature | Controllable variable
Time taken to puff | Controllable variable
Dough thickness | Constant
Entry angle | Observable outcome
assessment_items.question_text: A student categorises the factors in a puri investigation. Refer to the table provided. Which row contains an error in categorisation?

options.label: A
options.text: Dough thickness — it should be a controllable variable, not a constant

options.label: B
options.text: Entry angle — it should be a constant, not an observable outcome, but this is not an error if you choose to test it

options.label: C
options.text: Oil temperature — it should be a constant, not a controllable variable

options.label: D
options.text: Time taken to puff — it should be an observable outcome, not a controllable variable

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this reveals that the student does not yet distinguish between a variable that can be set by the investigator and one that is measured as a result — oil temperature is something the investigator sets deliberately.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this reveals the student may be thinking of dough thickness as something interesting to test rather than reading the scenario where it is deliberately held constant.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this reveals partial understanding — the student recognises entry angle can be a controllable variable but conflates this with it being correctly categorised as an observable outcome in this scenario.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find table-based questions difficult can be supported by first circling only the row they think might be wrong before reading the options. Students who answer readily can be asked to rewrite the table with one additional factor they would include and categorise it correctly.

assessment_items.stage_label: Identify Variables — distinguishing what can be changed, controlled, and observed
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can sort the factors of a given investigation into controllable variables, constants, and observable outcomes, and justify each placement using the distinction between what is changed and what is measured.

competency.competency_text: Formulate focused scientific questions, identify controllable and observable variables, design simple controlled experiments, and record observations systematically.

assessment_items.question_text: A student wants to investigate whether the size of the rolled dough circle affects whether a puri puffs. List two factors she must keep constant in this investigation and explain, in one sentence each, why keeping them constant is necessary.
expected_elements: Names at least two factors from the puri investigation (e.g. oil temperature, dough thickness, entry angle, flour type) as constants.
For each factor, provides a reason grounded in what would happen to the result if that factor varied — i.e. that the effect of dough-circle size could not be isolated.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find writing explanations difficult can respond with a labelled diagram showing the two trials side by side with annotations marking what is the same and what differs. Students with greater facility can be invited to name a third constant and explain which result it would contaminate if changed.

assessment_items.stage_label: Design a Controlled Experiment — applying the one-variable principle to plan a test
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can produce a written experimental plan that changes only one variable, specifies what is kept constant, and includes a recording scheme that captures both targeted measurements and unexpected observations, and can identify design flaws in another's plan.

competency.competency_text: Formulate focused scientific questions, identify controllable and observable variables, design simple controlled experiments, and record observations systematically.

assessment_items.question_text: A student plans to test whether oil temperature affects puffing time. In Trial 1 she uses low temperature oil and thin dough. In Trial 2 she uses high temperature oil and thick dough. She records only the puffing time in seconds. What is the most significant flaw in this plan?

options.label: A
options.text: She changed two variables between trials, so she cannot tell which one caused any difference in puffing time.

options.label: B
options.text: She did not record whether the oil splattered, so her results are incomplete.

options.label: C
options.text: She should have recorded puffing time in minutes, not seconds.

options.label: D
options.text: She should have used three oil temperatures instead of two.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this reveals the student is focused on measurement precision rather than experimental design — a valid concern in other contexts but not the primary flaw when two variables change simultaneously.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this reveals partial understanding of controlled experiments — more data points would improve the investigation, but the fundamental flaw of changing two variables at once is more serious and must be fixed first.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this reveals the student has absorbed the recording-completeness lesson but has applied it as the primary concern, when the more fundamental design flaw — changing two variables — makes the results uninterpretable regardless of how completely they are recorded.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to identify the flaw abstractly can be asked: 'If the puffing time is different between the two trials, how would you know whether temperature or dough thickness caused it?' — this concrete question often unlocks the recognition. Students who answer readily can be asked to rewrite the plan so it is valid.

assessment_items.stage_label: Design a Controlled Experiment — applying the one-variable principle to plan a test
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can produce a written experimental plan that changes only one variable, specifies what is kept constant, and includes a recording scheme that captures both targeted measurements and unexpected observations, and can identify design flaws in another's plan.

competency.competency_text: Formulate focused scientific questions, identify controllable and observable variables, design simple controlled experiments, and record observations systematically.

assessment_items.question_text: A student records only whether each puri puffed (yes or no) and ignores that the oil began to smoke during the last trial. According to the principles of scientific recording described in the chapter, what should she have done differently?

options.label: A
options.text: She should have recorded the smoking as an unexpected observation alongside her yes/no data, because unexpected details can seed new questions.

options.label: B
options.text: She should have repeated only the last trial so the smoking would not happen again.

options.label: C
options.text: She should have replaced yes/no with a numerical scale, since numbers are always more scientific than words.

options.label: D
options.text: She should have stopped the experiment when the oil began to smoke, as this means the results are invalid.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this reveals the misconception that unexpected events invalidate an experiment — the chapter explicitly frames such events as valuable data rather than evidence of failure.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this reveals the student treats the unexpected observation as a procedural problem to be eliminated rather than a scientific signal worth recording.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this reveals a confusion between measurement precision and recording completeness — numerical formats are useful but the chapter's point is about capturing unexpected qualitative details, not about replacing one format with another.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain can be prompted with: 'Would a scientist throw away any result they did not expect?' before selecting. Students who answer confidently can explain in one sentence how the smoking observation might lead to a new investigable question.

assessment_items.stage_label: Design a Controlled Experiment — applying the one-variable principle to plan a test
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can produce a written experimental plan that changes only one variable, specifies what is kept constant, and includes a recording scheme that captures both targeted measurements and unexpected observations, and can identify design flaws in another's plan.

competency.competency_text: Formulate focused scientific questions, identify controllable and observable variables, design simple controlled experiments, and record observations systematically.

assessment_items.question_text: Write a brief experimental plan to test whether oil temperature affects how long a puri takes to puff. Your plan must name (a) the one variable you change, (b) two factors you keep constant, and (c) two things you will record — one targeted measurement and one unexpected-detail column.
expected_elements: Names oil temperature as the variable being changed.
Names at least two constants drawn from the puri investigation (e.g. dough thickness, entry angle, flour type, puri size).
Names puffing time (or equivalent measurable outcome) as the targeted observation.
Names at least one unexpected-detail observation (e.g. whether oil splatters, smokes, or smells) as a separate recording column.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find prose planning difficult can present their plan as a two-column table (what changes / what stays the same) with a separate recording grid. Students with greater facility can be asked to explain why having both a targeted and an unexpected column makes the recording more scientifically complete.

assessment_items.stage_label: Iterate — using observations to generate new questions and refine investigations
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can identify a surprising finding in a set of investigation results, explain why it is unexpected in relation to the original question, and generate a new investigable question with a corresponding experimental plan that applies the one-variable and complete-recording principles.

competency.competency_text: Formulate focused scientific questions, identify controllable and observable variables, design simple controlled experiments, and record observations systematically.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Oil temperature | Puffing time (seconds) | Notes
Low | Did not puff | Oil appeared cool throughout
Medium | 8 | Puffed evenly

assessment_items.question_text: A student tests three oil temperatures and records her results. Refer to the table provided. Which finding is most surprising, and what new investigable question does it suggest?

options.label: A
options.text: High temperature caused smoking — suggesting the question: What type of oil smokes least?

options.label: B
options.text: Low temperature did not puff — suggesting the question: Does adding more oil help cold-temperature frying?

options.label: C
options.text: Medium temperature puffed evenly — suggesting the question: How can we make all puris puff evenly?

options.label: D
options.text: Medium temperature puffed faster than high temperature — suggesting the question: Why does higher temperature produce a slower or uneven puff?

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this reveals the student identified a result (no puffing at low temperature) that confirms expectations rather than challenges them — it is not the most surprising finding, and the follow-up question does not arise directly from the result.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this reveals the student focused on an unexpected detail from the notes column rather than on the primary outcome pattern — while smoking is a valid observation, the comparison between medium and high puffing times is the more scientifically productive surprise.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this reveals the student identified the positive result (medium puffed evenly) rather than the surprising comparison — the follow-up question is too broad to be investigable without further refinement.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find it difficult to identify 'surprising' can first be asked: 'What would you have expected to happen to puffing time as temperature goes up?' — establishing the expectation makes the surprise visible. Students who answer readily can be asked to design the follow-up experiment for option B in one sentence.

assessment_items.stage_label: Iterate — using observations to generate new questions and refine investigations
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can identify a surprising finding in a set of investigation results, explain why it is unexpected in relation to the original question, and generate a new investigable question with a corresponding experimental plan that applies the one-variable and complete-recording principles.

competency.competency_text: Formulate focused scientific questions, identify controllable and observable variables, design simple controlled experiments, and record observations systematically.

assessment_items.question_text: After completing an investigation into puri puffing, a student notices that the dough she stored overnight puffed much better than fresh dough she used the same morning. According to the chapter's view of scientific investigation, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Accept the stored dough as the better dough and use it in all future cooking without investigating further.

options.label: B
options.text: Discard this observation because it was not part of the original plan.

options.label: C
options.text: Frame 'Does storage time affect puffing?' as a new investigable question and design a follow-up investigation.

options.label: D
options.text: Report only the planned results and mention the fresh-versus-stored finding as a limitation.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this reveals the misconception that only planned observations count — the chapter explicitly states that unexpected observations are part of the record and often lead to the most productive new questions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this reveals a view of scientific investigation as a closed, report-and-finish activity rather than an iterative cycle — the student treats the unplanned finding as a flaw rather than a seed.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this reveals the student has drawn a practical conclusion from the observation without subjecting it to further investigation — a common confusion between using a result and investigating it.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who select option A or B can be asked to reread the chapter's fresh-versus-stored dough example before reconsidering. Students who answer readily can be asked to write the specific investigable question and name one variable they would change in the follow-up.

assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided, which shows results from a puri investigation. Identify the most surprising finding, explain in one sentence why it is unexpected, and write one new investigable question the results suggest.
expected_elements: Identifies the most surprising finding as older dough puffing faster (and more evenly) than fresh dough, or the consistent decrease in puffing time with storage age.
Explains why this is unexpected — e.g. one might have expected fresh dough to perform better because it is newer or more active.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can evaluate a given investigation against the full scientific inquiry cycle — identifying strengths and flaws in question formulation, variable control, observation recording, and iteration — and propose a specific improvement for each identified flaw.

assessment_items.question_text: A student investigating whether dough thickness affects puffing time changes the thickness between trials but also uses a different flour type in each trial. She records only the puffing time in seconds and concludes that thicker dough puffs more slowly. Which evaluation of her investigation is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Her conclusion is reliable because she compared two trials directly.

options.label: B
options.text: Her conclusion may be wrong because she changed two variables, making it impossible to attribute the result to dough thickness alone.

options.label: C
options.text: Her investigation is flawed only because she did not record unexpected observations such as splattering.

options.label: D
options.text: Her investigation is sound because she recorded a numerical measurement.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this reveals the student equates numerical measurement with scientific validity — a common conflation that misses the more fundamental issue of variable control.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this reveals the student has isolated one dimension of good scientific practice (complete recording) but applied it as the primary flaw rather than recognising that the two-variable design problem makes the conclusion unreliable regardless of recording completeness.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this reveals the student treats direct comparison as sufficient for a valid conclusion — missing that the comparison is contaminated by the simultaneous change in flour type.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to evaluate the whole investigation can be asked to answer two simpler questions first: 'Did she change one variable or two?' and 'Does that affect whether her conclusion is reliable?' before engaging with the option set. Students who answer readily can be asked to restate a corrected version of her conclusion given the flaw.

assessment_items.question_text: After completing her puri investigation, a student writes: 'My results show what I expected, so the experiment is finished.' According to the scientific inquiry principles in the chapter, what is the most important thing missing from this conclusion?

options.label: A
options.text: She has not compared her results with those of a classmate.

options.label: B
options.text: She has not considered what new questions the results open for a follow-up investigation.

options.label: C
options.text: She has not converted her observations into a graph.

options.label: D
options.text: She has not repeated the experiment at least three times.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this reveals the student associates scientific validity with graphical representation — while graphs are useful, the chapter does not present them as a required closure step and the specific gap here is iterative thinking.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this reveals a procedural association — repeated trials are good practice but the chapter's central argument is about the iterative generation of new questions, not about the number of repetitions.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this reveals an association between peer comparison and scientific completeness — peer review has value, but it is not the specific iterative principle the chapter emphasises as the defining feature of investigation.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who select a distractor can be redirected by asking: 'What does the chapter say happens after you complete one round of experiments?' Students who answer readily can be asked to write the specific new question her results should have generated.

assessment_items.question_text: Read the following account of a student's investigation and evaluate it fully. Riya wants to know what affects puri puffing. She fries three puris — one with thin dough at low temperature, one with medium dough at medium temperature, and one with thick dough at high temperature. She records only whether each puri puffed (yes or no). After the third puri puffs, she concludes: 'Thick dough at high temperature is best for puffing.' She considers the investigation complete. Identify and explain two specific flaws in Riya's investigation and propose one concrete improvement for each flaw.
look_for: Identifies the two-variable-change flaw: Riya changed both dough thickness and oil temperature simultaneously in each trial, making it impossible to attribute the puffing outcome to either variable alone.
Identifies the recording-completeness flaw: recording only yes/no does not capture the degree of puffing, the time taken, or any unexpected observations such as splattering or smoking.
Proposes a concrete improvement for the two-variable flaw — e.g. fix dough thickness and vary only oil temperature across three trials, or fix temperature and vary only thickness.
Proposes a concrete improvement for the recording flaw — e.g. add a column for puffing time in seconds and a column for unexpected observations.
Optionally identifies the closure flaw — treating the investigation as finished without asking what new question the result opens — as a third flaw with a corresponding suggestion.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find unstructured extended writing difficult can be given a two-row table with headers 'Flaw' and 'Improvement' to fill in rather than writing in continuous prose. Students with greater facility can be asked to rewrite Riya's full investigation plan so that it is valid, including a recording sheet design.

assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided, which summarises four aspects of a student's puri investigation. For each row: (1) decide whether it represents a flaw or a strength in Arjun's investigation, (2) name the inquiry criterion it relates to, and (3) if it is a flaw, write a specific improvement. Then, in two or three sentences at the bottom of your response, explain how the inquiry cycle — from question through variable control, recording, and iteration — works as an integrated whole rather than a checklist of separate steps.
assessment_items.scaffold: Work through each row of the table one at a time before writing your overall explanation. For the iteration row, ask yourself: what does the chapter say should happen after one round of experiments is complete?
format_of_output: Completed table with flaw/strength, criterion, and improvement columns filled in for each of the four rows.
Two-to-three sentence written explanation of how the inquiry cycle works as an integrated whole.

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Procedure evaluation task (identify flaw, suggest improvement)
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The Final Stage implied LO requires the student to evaluate an investigation across all four inquiry criteria and propose improvements — a procedure evaluation task is the most direct demonstration vehicle for this multi-criterion evaluative operation.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response evidences the student's ability to apply the full scientific inquiry cycle as an integrated evaluative lens — assessing question quality, variable control, recording completeness, and iterative thinking simultaneously on a single investigation account, and proposing specific improvements rather than generic ones.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The table structure ensures all four inquiry criteria are assessed; a student who fills in only two or three rows has not demonstrated full-cycle evaluation. The final written explanation is the synthesis move — it is where the student shows they understand the criteria as interconnected rather than independent. A student who lists correct table entries but writes a generic or circular explanation has demonstrated procedural but not integrated understanding.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: name the specific flaw in each flawed row (e.g. 'He stopped after one result without asking what new question it opens'), propose a concrete improvement tied to that specific flaw, and write an explanation that connects at least two criteria causally (e.g. 'Poor variable control makes recording useless because you cannot attribute what you measured to the right cause'). Weak responses: label rows correctly but propose improvements that are too vague ('he should do it better') or write a summary explanation that simply lists the four criteria without explaining how they interact.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the written explanation difficult can first talk through it with a partner and then write one sentence instead of three. Students with greater facility can be asked to add a fifth row to the table — one they design themselves — representing a different aspect of investigation quality not covered by the four given rows.
